name: Drawn in Japan: Manga, Anime and Their Global Reach
description: How a monster film, a robot boy and a weekly magazine grew into worldwide fandom, from Astro Boy and Godzilla to Studio Ghibli, One Piece and Pokémon.

checkpoints.name: Cards, reels and a monster
checkpoints.note: Nintendo begins in 1889 as a maker of playing cards, and anime starts as short animated films in the 1910s. After the war, Osamu Tezuka launches Astro Boy in 1952, and the studio Toho sends Godzilla stomping through Tokyo in 1954, giving Japan a robot hero and a monster.

checkpoints.name: Magazines and mascots
checkpoints.note: Weekly Shonen Jump starts in 1968 and becomes a home for serial adventures read by millions of young people. Doraemon, a robot cat from the future, arrives in 1969, Hello Kitty appears in 1974, and Yellow Magic Orchestra brings synthesizer pop out of Tokyo in 1978.

checkpoints.name: Consoles, epics and a studio
checkpoints.note: Akira begins as a manga in 1982 and Dragon Ball in 1984. Nintendo's home console arrives in 1983 (as the NES abroad) and Super Mario Bros follows in 1985, the year Studio Ghibli is founded. Oshin, a long NHK morning drama, becomes a national favourite.

checkpoints.name: Fans around the world
checkpoints.note: Sailor Moon (1991), Detective Conan (1994), One Piece (1997) and Naruto (1999) each run for years and are translated into many languages. Spirited Away (2001), from Studio Ghibli, later wins an Academy Award, and Death Note (2003) shows a dark thriller can sell too.

checkpoints.name: On every screen
checkpoints.note: Pokémon Go, released in 2016, puts a Japanese monster-collecting franchise onto phones around the world, a sign of how far these characters have travelled. Magazines still serialise new stories, while streaming carries anime to audiences in many countries.
